Transcript Body:
[00:00] Jordan: all right everyone thanks for joining uh from Redwood, I'm Jordan — I'm the AE on the account, and with me is Priya and Alex on the solutions side. how's everyone doing?
[00:05] Carlos: good yeah thanks for setting this up Jordan. we've been looking at inference costs closely, this quarter budget's — it's pretty tight so we need to map unit economics before we commit.
[00:12] Leah: yeah hi, Leah here. we'll be the ML owners, largely responsible for prompt optimization and embeddings for reranking.
[00:17] Omar: Omar, SRE — I care about SLOs and networking for private deployments.
[00:21] Jordan: awesome. quick goal for this call: understand your traffic and latency targets, talk through the levers — batching, K V cache, quantization — and outline a pilot and benchmarks so you can see concrete numbers. is that right on your side?
[00:30] Carlos: yes exactly. also procurement wants a rough hosted vs dedicated spend comparison, and we need to know what will be stable month-to-month.
[00:36] Jordan: got it. uh, Priya, do you want to start with the traffic profile we asked for?
[00:40] Priya: sure. so from the notes we got, Sequoia is planning a routing ETA microservice, 60% of calls are short prompts ~ 40–60 tokens, 30% mid (200 tokens), 10% long (up to 1024 tokens) for detailed logs. Peak is around 600 rps during rush windows, average steady-state is 120 rps. Does that still match?
[01:02] Leah: yes that's right; also about 20% of calls are embedding lookups for reranking, those are cheap per-call but frequent.
[01:09] Priya: perfect. so two primary levers for per-token cost: batching (amortizing model init and kernel overhead across requests) and KV/prefix caching for repeated context. for routing you get a lot of repeated prefixes — we can probably cache that.
[01:23] Carlos: when you say cache, is that like a session cache? how persistent is the K V?
[01:27] Alex: good question — our KV cache stores decoded KV tensors for a pinned model variant and is sticky per shard. TTLs are configurable; for user-facing repeated prefixes we often set a short TTL (seconds) to hit the cache on burst traffic. basically it avoids re-attending to the prefix and saves token ops.
[01:42] Omar: and is that available on Hosted and Dedicated? or only private?
[01:46] Priya: KV caching is available across Hosted and Dedicated. for Private we hand over more control to your infra; you'll be able to tune TTLs and pin caches in your environment. note though that cross-instance cache hits depend on routing — if requests hit different GPU pools you might not hit the cache unless you use sticky routing or a shared cache layer.
[02:06] Leah: okay got it. can you give a rough per-token number for the model we're evaluating? we had been testing Mistral-XXL-open variant in house.
[02:13] Priya: rough ranges: for that model on our hosted profile, raw generation cost is approximately $0.00035–$0.0005 per token depending on batching and sequence length. with effective batching and KV cache for short prompts we often see effective per-token drop to $0.00018–$0.00025. these are ballpark — we'll run your replay to get concrete.
[02:35] Carlos: that's a wide range. what drives the lower bound — is it quantization?
[02:39] Priya: quantization helps; we also have smaller model variants for lower-cost fallbacks — e.g., a quantized 8-bit variant for bulk inference. but the biggest wins for routing workloads are batching and cache hits. if 60% of requests are similar and hit the prefix cache, your average token cost plummets because you avoid re-computing the expensive prefix.
[02:55] Omar: latency — if we increase batch sizes to save money, do we risk missing our 200ms 95th SLO?
[03:00] Priya: this is the classic tradeoff. Redwood's runtime has adaptive batching: we set a max batch window and a target latency. you can configure a policy that caps batch delay at e.g., 8–12ms for user-facing low-latency calls to keep P95 tight. for longer background jobs you can use bigger windows. Dedicated gives you more predictable batch formation because you control concurrency, but hosted also supports low-latency policies.
[03:21] Leah: so Dedicated helps predictability — is that mostly cost predictability or latency?
[03:26] Jordan: both. Dedicated gives you reserved capacity and isolation so variance from noisy neighbors is minimized. cost-wise you trade usage-based for reserved commitments (monthly), which helps forecasting but requires a commit. Hosted is flexible but month-to-month spend can fluctuate with traffic.
[03:40] Carlos: procurement wants to know break-even — when does dedicated make sense? we have an internal finance threshold of steady spend ~ $80k/month to consider reserved capacity.
[03:47] Alex: typical break-even depends on your token volumes and desired SLOs. we can run a model: take your replay, apply our hosted per-token pricing with observed cache & batching hit rates, then show a dedicated commitment curve. that's part of the benchmark deliverable.
[03:59] Omar: about security — we need SOC2, SSO, audit logs, and KMS integration. is that standard?
[04:04] Priya: yes SOC2 Type II is standard for Redwood hosted. we support SSO/SAML and RBAC. for Private deployments we integrate with customer KMS/HSM for key management and you get full audit logs in your VPC. we'll share the security pack.
[04:16] Carlos: and data residency? some logs can't leave EU. we have EU customers for part of our fleet.
[04:20] Jordan: we have region-specific hosting and can pin inference to EU regions; for strict residency you'd look at Private or Dedicated in an EU region — we can map that.
[04:29] Leah: ok practical question — if we run the replay and see average found cost $0.00022 per token on hosted with 40% cache hit, what's the improvement path? do you have recommended prompt changes?
[04:39] Priya: yes — typical playbook: 1) reduce prompt tokens via templating and placeholder tokens, 2) move static context to KV cache or embeddings store, 3) use smaller models or quantized variants for low-criticality steps, 4) optimize batch sizing with micro-batching to hit throughput without harming latency. we'll share a prompt optimization checklist.
[04:56] Carlos: what's the friction for switching from hosted to private later? we might start hosted, then commit to private when we hit scale.
[05:02] Jordan: the API and model catalog are consistent across modes; the main friction is networking and KMS set up for Private plus any audit/compliance gating. we support a migration path where you can pin model versions and configs; we also do a performance rebaseline because hardware/quantization may differ. it's often straightforward but requires an infra window and testing.
[05:20] Omar: on the private side, we have an air-gapped environment for certain customers. does Redwood support on-prem air-gapped deployments?
[05:26] Priya: yes, there's an on-prem package — it's more involved (install, test, continuous updates strategy), and it includes manual steps around model updates and telemetry. we can provide an ops runbook.
[05:36] Carlos: back to costs — your pilot pricing for a 4-week pilot, what does that look like?
[05:40] Jordan: we usually offer a pilot plan: fixed-fee up to a certain token cap plus optional overage. for example, we can do a 4-week pilot priced at $15k covering up to X tokens with a performance benchmark included. we'll tailor based on your replay.
[05:56] Leah: you mentioned fallbacks to smaller models — how do you manage quality regressions? do you have A/B or canary?
[06:01] Alex: yes, Redwood supports rollout policies — canary, A/B, and automated fallback when latency or error thresholds are breached. we also integrate quality monitoring tied to prompt sets so you can detect regressions.
[06:12] Carlos: perfect. Procurement: "Priya" from our side — what are the billing terms?
[06:16] Priya (customer): we need net-30 and an invoice to the EU entity. also will you provide a pricing comparison spreadsheet?
[06:21] Jordan: yes, net-30 is fine for pilot. I'll include hosted vs dedicated pro-forma for a few commitment tiers.
[06:26] Omar: quick technical — if we want sticky routing to preserve cache hits, do you provide session affinity?
[06:31] Priya (Redwood SE): we have routing policies supporting sticky sessions by user id or request hash. you can configure per-route policies in the console or via API. note that sticky routing reduces some elasticity but improves cache localities.
[06:44] Leah: in the replay, we have bursts that are 10–12x baseline. how does autoscaling behave in Hosted vs Dedicated?
[06:51] Alex: hosted autoscaling is fast but shared pool may hit quota limits; Dedicated gives reserved headroom and predictable scaling within your pool. we also offer burst capacity add-ons to augment reserved pools for short spikes.
[07:05] Carlos: can we get an expected P95 latency number per model variant at our observed 600 rps peak?
[07:11] Priya: yes — we'll run the 2-hour benchmark at peak and provide P50/P95/P99 and cost breakdown per-token and per-response. That will include breakdowns by token type (prompt tokens vs generated tokens), batching efficiency, and cache hit rate.
[07:24] Jordan: just to set expectations, benchmarks are reproducible but dependent on sequence length distribution and request interarrival patterns; we'll model both average and worst-case.
[07:33] Omar: if we need private deployment, what logs do we get? I need request-level audit + token accounting.
[07:38] Priya: Private gives you full audit logs with token-level accounting and can export to your SIEM. Hosted provides token-level usage too, but for strict compliance we recommend Private or Dedicated with extended retention.
[07:50] Carlos: are there hidden costs — e.g., for KV cache storage or telemetry exports?
[07:54] Jordan: telemetry exports beyond the included retention are an add-on; KV caching within the runtime is included but large-scale externalized cache layers could be billed if they require extra infra. we'll make those explicit in the pilot pricing sheet.
[08:05] Leah: edge case — if a bunch of our traffic is embeddings-heavy, are embeddings priced differently?
[08:09] Priya: yes embeddings are priced per embedding unit; generally cheaper than generation per token for most models. we'll include that in the cost breakdown.
[08:16] Carlos: OK let's recap next steps verbally.
[08:18] Jordan: recap: 1) Jordan will send pilot pricing + hosted vs dedicated comparison and contract skeleton by Friday 2027-10-08. 2) Sequoia shares 72h request logs and sample prompt sets by Monday 2027-10-10. 3) Priya (Redwood) will run 2-hour and a peak replay benchmark and return results by 2027-10-13. 4) Schedule private deployment deep-dive with Omar week of 2027-10-18. Anything else?
[08:42] Carlos: that covers it from our side. procurement will review the pilot fee.
[08:46] Priya (customer): we might need a small NDA tweak but procurement will flag that separately.
[08:50] Jordan: great — we'll follow up in email with links to the SOC2 pack, SDK quickstart, and the pricing spreadsheet. thanks everyone.
[08:55] Leah: thanks all.
[08:56] Omar: thanks.
